Patient Note:
A 35-year-old Japanese man with a history of renal disease presented to a dermatology clinic with sudden onset of a purpuric rash on his lower extremities () and was diagnosed with anaphylactoid purpura. Although he was asymptomatic, proteinuria, and haematuria were detected during a screening test when he was 20 years old, and he was diagnosed with IgAN based on renal biopsy. Histopathological examination of renal biopsy specimens revealed mild mesangial proliferation (). Immunohistochemical examination revealed mesangial IgA (), IgG and C3 () depositions, and he was treated with corticosteroids. Thereafter, he moved to our city and continued to be treated here. Corticosteroids treatment was continued for 7 years and was subsequently tapered.
Physical examination following the appearance of purpura revealed purpuric rash without any pitting oedema on his legs. Blood pressure was 147/78 mmHg. Urinalysis showed (+++) urinary protein, no urinary glucose, 6–10 red blood cells/high power field, urinary protein was 1.4 g/g creatinine (Cr). A peripheral blood smear showed a white blood cell (WBC) count of 12,100 cells/mm3, red blood cell of 5.16 million cells/mm3, and platelets 192,000 cells/mm3. Serum haemoglobin was 16.6 g/dL and haematocrit 45.4%. Blood chemistry showed total serum protein 7.2 g/dL, serum albumin 4.2 g/dL, serum sodium 141 mEq/L, potassium 4.3 mEq/L, chloride 105 mEq/L, serum Cr 1.35 mg/dL, serum aspartate aminotransferase 21 IU/L, serum alanine aminotransferase 28 IU/L, blood glucose 96 mg/dL, glycosylated haemoglobin 4.8%, and serum C-reactive protein (CRP) 1.57 mg/dL. Immunological examination showed an antistreptolysin O (ASO) titer 24 IU/mL, IgG 1095 mg/dL, IgA 315 mg/dL, IgM 133 mg/dL, C3 164 mg/dL, C4 35 mg/dL, and CH50 67.0 U/mL.

Patient Note:
A three-year-old male with a history of obstructive sleep apnea presented to the pediatric emergency department (PED) on postoperative day (POD) three with a chief complaint of hematemesis. The morning of presentation, the patient awoke fussy and subsequently began to vomit. His mother witnessed a clot in the emesis with frank hematemesis with continued bleeding coming from the oropharynx, and she transported him via personal vehicle to the hospital. Upon arrival, the patient was afebrile at 37.5ºC, with a heart rate of 137 beats per minute, respiratory rate of 28 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation of 98% on room air, blood pressure of 111/85 millimeters mercury (mm Hg), and weight of 12 kilograms (kg). On exam, the patient appeared pale and tachycardic with active retching, and with blood pooled in the posterior oropharynx that obscured visualization of the tonsillar beds.
A complete blood count (CBC), coagulation profile, and type and cross were obtained, and ondansetron was administered intravenously (IV). A cold-water rinse was attempted; however, the patient did not tolerate this intervention. Nebulized TXA was administered by using 250 milligrams (mg) (50mg/per milliliter) IV solution via direct nebulization at a flow rate of eight liters over four minutes without additive of normal saline solution. After administration of TXA, the patient had no obvious bleeding from the posterior pharynx and his retching improved. He was then admitted to the general pediatric inpatient service for further monitoring with pediatric otolaryngology (ENT) consultation. The CBC and coagulation studies were within the normal range on admission with hemoglobin 12.0 grams per deciliter (gm/dL) (normal range 11.5–14.5 gm/dL), prothrombin time (PT) 13.8 seconds (sec) (11.7–14.7 sec), and partial thromboplastin time (PTT) 33.3 sec (25–35 sec).
These lab tests were not repeated during his hospitalization. After an initial refusal of oral intake requiring maintenance IV fluids the patient was able to be transitioned to a soft diet, which he tolerated, and he was discharged on hospital day three. He had no further bleeding, and no adverse effects from nebulized TXA were documented. The patient’s initial surgery was performed at an outside facility, and no follow-up visits were done at our institution for review.

Patient Note:
A 57-year-old woman presented with a two-day history of significantly reduced urine output accompanied by mild fatigue and generalized weakness. She reported feeling more lethargic than usual over the past week, with a noticeable decrease in her usual fluid intake due to intermittent nausea. Her medical history includes hypertension, for which she was started on a new medication six months ago, and well-controlled type 2 diabetes, although she admits to occasional lapses in medication adherence. She denies recent fevers, chills, or respiratory symptoms. On initial examination, she appeared tired but alert and oriented. Her vital signs revealed a mildly elevated heart rate and borderline low blood pressure, with moderate jugular venous distension that fluctuated upon repeated assessments. Inspection of her extremities suggested subtle peripheral edema, and her skin turgor was reduced, which raised questions regarding her overall fluid balance. Cardiopulmonary examination revealed no abnormal murmurs, but she did exhibit a soft S4 gallop consistent with a long-standing history of controlled hypertension. She reported no chest pain or palpitations. Abdominal examination was unremarkable aside from mild right-sided flank tenderness on deep palpation, but she had no guarding or rebound tenderness. She expressed concerns about her reduced oral intake and admitted uncertainty about whether she had received adequate hydration in the days leading up to her presentation. At the time of arrival, laboratory results demonstrated an elevated serum creatinine measured at 1.4 mg/dL, up from her reported baseline of approximately 0.9 mg/dL, suggesting an acute change in renal function. Her serum sodium concentration was recorded at 138 mEq/L, which falls within normal limits, though on the slightly higher end of her typical range. Urinalysis showed no significant hematuria or heavy proteinuria, but subsequent measurement revealed a urinary sodium level around 28 mEq/L, which prompted further contemplation regarding possible prerenal causes versus intrinsic renal pathology. Her urine creatinine was 105 mg/dL, pointing to a concentrated specimen at the time of collection. She remains oliguric, passing minimal volumes of dark, concentrated fluid, although she has not reported flank pain outside of the mild discomfort elicited during the abdominal examination. Previous outpatient records suggest that multiple factors could have predisposed her to this episode, including the possibility of transient hypotension or decreased effective circulating volume, given her modest daily fluid intake. In addition, she recalls multiple episodes of diarrhea last week, possibly contributing to volume depletion. She denies taking any over-the-counter nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs recently and reports no known exposure to nephrotoxic agents, although she did acknowledge sporadic use of an herbal supplement she could not fully identify. A thorough review of her current medications, including her antihypertensives, is underway to determine whether recent medication adjustments had a role in this abrupt decline in kidney function. She has no notable rash or joint swelling that might suggest a systemic inflammatory process. Despite mild orthostatic changes, she has had no recorded syncope or major cardiovascular events. She indicates that this is the first time she has experienced such a pronounced decrease in urine output, and she expresses concern about whether her kidneys are permanently affected. She remains under close observation, with plans for careful fluid assessment and possible imaging studies to rule out obstructive causes. Her care team is also considering additional workup to distinguish between prerenal and intrinsic factors, as well as evaluating whether her medications may have contributed to an acute disruption of renal hemodynamics. The patient’s primary goal remains to determine the cause of her markedly diminished urine production while addressing potential underlying triggers, and she is agreeable to further diagnostic testing to elucidate any reversible elements contributing to her current condition.

Patient Note:
A now four-year-old boy presented at the age of 3 years to our emergency department with a 2-week history of fever (39.5 °C), vomiting, and watery stools, which had already improved. He also had lower limb oedema and periorbital puffiness for one week. Apart from receiving paracetamol for the fever, there was no history of medication use. He is the offspring of parents in a consanguineous marriage with an unremarkable past medical history. He has one sister and three brothers. One of his brothers was diagnosed with steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome due to membranous proliferative glomerulonephritis (MPGN) with C3 deposition diagnosed by kidney biopsy at 3 years of age. He reached chronic kidney disease stage 5 at the age of 4 years. Dialysis was considered, but he died in another hospital due to sepsis. No genetic testing was done on his brother.
On initial examination, the patient was stable but hypertensive with blood pressure reading of 136/83 mmHg, generalized oedema and a distended abdomen. No other abnormalities detected in systemic examinations. Laboratory investigations were performed and revealed the following: serum creatinine (45 µmol/L; normal 2.6–52.2 µmol/L), blood urea nitrogen (14.1 mmol/L; normal 1.8–6.4 mmol/L), potassium (5.5 mmol/L), sodium (135 mmol/L), chloride (110 mmol/L), bicarbonate (18 mmol/L), albumin (1.2 g/dL; normal 3.4-4.2 g/dL), haemoglobin (Hgb) (5.2 g/dL; normal 11.5–14.5 g/dL), white blood cell (WBC) count (9.13 × 109/L; normal 4–12 × 109/L), platelet count (23 × 109/L; normal 150–400 × 109/L), haptoglobin (< 0.058 g/L; normal 0.5–2.2 g/L), lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) (1425 U/L; normal 150–500 U/L), complement C3 (C3) (0.550 g/L; normal 0.80–1.60 g/L), and complement C4 (C4) (0.109/L; normal 0.16–0.48 g/L). The patient also had normal coagulation profile, normal level of ADAMTS13, negative coombs test and peripheral blood smears showed schistocytes. His urine dipstick showed urine protein excretion of > 400 mg/dL and 20–50 red blood cells/high power field. Stool cultures and analysis revealed no pathogens (Table ). Due to his uncontrolled hypertension and thrombocytopenia, the patient could not undergo a kidney biopsy.
The patient’s clinical picture fit the diagnosis of aHUS, and eculizumab was started within 24 h of the diagnosis. Following the recommendations of the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the manufacturer, he was given a 600 mg intravenous (IV) infusion as induction therapy and a 300 mg IV infusion every two weeks as maintenance therapy. After two doses of eculizumab, he started to show clinical and laboratory improvement. His Hgb improved to 9 g/dL; his platelet count increased to 169 × 109/L; and his C3, haptoglobin, and LDH levels were normalized (Table ). His blood pressure was controlled on amlodipine and lisinopril, and his oedema significantly improved. A genetic panel for aHUS was performed, and the patient showed a homozygous nonsense gene mutation in DGKE p.(Phe250Serfs*3). No mutation was detected in the gene coding regions of ADAMTS13, C3, CD46, CFB, CFH, CFHR1, CFHR2, CFHR3, CFHR5, CFI, MMACHC, PIGA, PLG, THBD, CD59, CR1, CR2, INF2, or MUT.
Six months after presentation, the patient was stable and in clinical remission on eculizumab 300 mg every other week. His laboratory parameters were within the normal ranges (Hgb 11.8 g/dL, platelet count 543 × 109/L, C3 0.9 g/L) apart from persistent moderate proteinuria, with urine dipstick 100 mg/dL and serum albumin 2.5 g/dL (Table ). Based on the genetic results and the patient’s general condition, we decided to start increasing the time between eculizumab doses, targeting discontinuation. A 300 mg IV infusion of eculizumab was administered every three weeks instead of every two weeks. Following the first dose after increasing the time between doses, the patient was noticed to be oedematous; his proteinuria in urine dipstick increased to 400 − 300 mg/dL with urine protein/creatinine ratio > 3 mg/mg, his albumin dropped to 1.9 g/dL, and other laboratory parameters, including Hgb and platelet count, were within the normal ranges (Hgb 12.2 g/dl and platelet count 494 × 109/L) (Table ). His oedema improved after the addition of oral furosemide at 1 mg/kg/dose twice daily. Nevertheless, after 4 months of eculizumab every 3 weeks, the patient’s proteinuria and albumin levels did not improve. The decision was made to try eculizumab every two weeks and observe his proteinuria. Interestingly, his proteinuria improved to 100 mg/dL after only two doses of the two-week regimen, his oedema subsided and serum albumin improved gradually from 1.9 g/L to 2.2 g/L (Table ). Four months later, patient is stable on eculizumab 300 mg IV infusion every two weeks with no oedema and stable proteinuria and Albumin (Table ). Throughout his first year after presentation, apart from proteinuria, his creatinine was within the normal range, and he had no signs of HUS activity after the first remission.

Patient Note:
A 74-year-old female arrived at the hospital complaining of a three-day history of progressively worsening cough, which she described as initially dry but recently accompanied by scant sputum production. She reported a notable surge in body temperature, measured at 102.4 degrees Fahrenheit on the morning of presentation, and expressed concern about rising fevers over the past several days. She described experiencing intermittent chills and increasing fatigue, particularly when attempting her usual household tasks. Although she occasionally finds it difficult to climb stairs due to a history of heart-related issues that require vigilance for fluid accumulation, she has managed her condition with periodic medical follow-up and close attention to her diet and daily weight checks. She mentioned that her breathing had become more labored than normal, and she found herself short of breath even with minimal exertion, such as walking across her living room. She denied any chronic issues suggestive of long-term kidney dysfunction and stated that her serum chemistry panels have historically been within acceptable ranges. She further explained that she had never been given a diagnosis of a serious or malignant condition, and she did not recall any episode in her life involving sudden neurologic symptoms like one-sided weakness, difficulty speaking, or transient blindness. Her daily living routine had been largely independent, and she resided in her own home without the need for extended care or specialized assistance. Upon examination in the emergency department, her vital signs included a heart rate of 97 beats per minute, a systolic blood pressure of 125 mm Hg, a respiratory rate of 25 breaths per minute, and the aforementioned elevated temperature. She indicated feeling somewhat lightheaded when ambulating, but she was able to communicate effectively and did not appear to be in any obvious distress apart from her labored breathing. Laboratory investigations performed before starting any treatment revealed a blood urea nitrogen value of 23 mg/dL, which she was informed is on the higher end of normal but does not necessarily suggest a chronic problem, especially in the absence of other concerning findings. Serum electrolytes showed a sodium measurement of 135 mEq/L, which was considered acceptable for her age and clinical status. Her glucose level at presentation was 115 mg/dL, which did not raise immediate concern for a significant metabolic derangement. A measurement of hematocrit at 40% was documented, indicating that her red blood cell concentration was not substantially reduced. Arterial blood sampling disclosed a normal acid-base balance, with a pH of 7.43, and her partial pressure of oxygen was found to be 86 mm Hg on room air, illustrating that she might need close observation for possible hypoxemia. Further evaluation included a chest imaging study that demonstrated evidence of infection in the lung fields and a clear indication of excess fluid layering within the pleural space. The presence of additional fluid raised the suspicion that her background of heart problems, which she stated had led to occasional lower extremity swelling and prior episodes of reduced exercise tolerance, could predispose her to more complications. However, she denied any knowledge of prior significant events beyond her known cardiovascular condition and maintained that she had not sought care for pneumonia in the past. She explained that her appetite had been poor for the last few days, possibly related to her persistent fever and cough, but she remained adequately hydrated at home. On auscultation, her lungs revealed diminished breath sounds and localized crackles in an area consistent with the imaging findings, supporting the possibility of an infectious and inflammatory process. Despite her clear signs of a pulmonary issue, she neither reported confusion nor appeared disoriented during assessment. Presenting data suggested no major disturbance in other organ systems, and she emphasized that she had never received any ongoing treatments aimed at controlling major chronic illnesses aside from her known cardiac difficulties. Her clinical team decided that she would require further in-hospital investigation and supportive measures for what appeared to be a significant respiratory tract infection, given her fever, compromised breathing, and lab results captured at the time of admission.

Patient Note:
A 53-year-old female was brought to the emergency department by ambulance after slipping on a wet floor at her workplace earlier in the day. Witnesses reported that she lost her balance while carrying a box of office supplies, landing primarily on her right side and briefly complaining of soreness in the right arm and hip. She did not report any immediate loss of consciousness, but coworkers noted that she appeared somewhat shaken, prompting them to call for emergency assistance out of concern for potential head or spinal injury. On arrival at the hospital, she was seated upright on the gurney and maintained her gaze toward staff members entering the room without any prompting, suggesting that she was responsive to her environment. During the initial examination, she was engaged in clear dialogue with the nurse, accurately detailing her name, the current date, and the nature of her workday, as well as explaining the sequence of events leading up to the fall. She recalled precisely what she had been doing and appeared receptive to questions, answering them cogently and with appropriate detail. When queried about her surroundings, she could identify that she was in the hospital and recognized it as the local facility nearest to her workplace. She continued to interact in a calm, coherent manner, showing no sign of confusional states or hesitation in speech. As the clinician proceeded with the neurological assessment, she responded promptly to each request, including moving her arms and legs when asked, thereby allowing the evaluator to check for any focal deficits or signs of weakness. Although she mentioned mild discomfort in her right hip and wrist, she did not demonstrate any difficulty completing simple tasks such as extending both arms or flexing her knees. The positional changes did not elicit additional pain, though she did briefly note mild tenderness around her right femoral region when palpated. Further examination of her cranial nerves did not reveal any abnormality; her pupils were equal and reactive, ocular movements were aligned, and there was no facial drooping or asymmetry in her smile. She voiced an ability to feel light touch and pressure on her upper and lower extremities without issue, and she could localize gentle tactile stimuli. Her vital signs on admission were stable, with blood pressure slightly elevated but still within a reasonable range, which she attributed to feeling anxious after the fall. She denied any nausea, vomiting, or dizziness, though she did admit to feeling somewhat stiff and achy from the impact of the fall. Laboratory tests were ordered to rule out any underlying problems, and imaging studies of her hip and wrist were requested to ensure there were no fractures or significant soft tissue injuries. She reported a past medical history of lower back discomfort for which she occasionally took over-the-counter analgesics, but she stated she had no chronic neurological conditions, had never undergone surgery, and did not have any major medical diagnoses such as diabetes or hypertension. She also denied any known allergies. In fact, she described her overall health as generally good, explaining that she usually remains quite active, walking or cycling when weather permits. By the time the clinical team completed this initial assessment, she continued to respond willingly and accurately to all questions, showed consistent awareness of people around her, and readily moved each limb when asked, reinforcing the impression that she had remained cognitively intact throughout the event and retained full voluntary control of her extremities despite the tumble earlier in the day.

Patient Note:
A 58-year-old female arrives with concerns about an upcoming minimally invasive joint procedure that utilizes specialized instruments and small incisions to manage persistent knee pain and mechanical symptoms. The patient reports experiencing a neurologic deficit within the last few weeks that required urgent medical attention and some rehabilitative support, though motor function and overall coordination have largely improved under close supervision. Vital signs at presentation are within acceptable limits, and the patient denies any recent history of large-scale or extensive surgical interventions. The cardiovascular review reveals no new or recurring manifestations of compromised cardiac output or systemic fluid buildup in recent days, and the patient also indicates no serious bloodstream complications requiring hospital-level management during the same period. There is no account of major traumatic injuries imparting widespread bodily harm, and the patient does not recall any recent fractures involving the hip, pelvis, or lower limbs. Examination of both legs shows no enlarged superficial vessels, and the patient reports no swelling or discomfort suggestive of fluid retention in the calves or thighs at this time. Currently, there is a vascular access line in place that was established for easier administration of intravenous therapies, which remains functional and has shown no signs of infection or malfunction on inspection. Notably, the patient acknowledges a previous episode of a clot in a deep vein that required targeted treatment in the past, yet denies any prior episode where a clot dislodged and traveled to the pulmonary circulation. When asked about inherited or acquired factors that can heighten the likelihood of forming problematic clots, the patient mentions having undergone evaluations in earlier years but never testing positive for abnormalities associated with heightened thrombosis risk. This includes the absence of any significant indicators for specific genetic or autoimmune processes that might predispose to excessive clot formation. The patient likewise denies a personal history of conditions affecting the bowel or requiring regular monitoring for chronic inflammatory symptoms, and there have been no recent signs pointing toward an acute cardiac event involving the coronary arteries. Self-reported daily functioning suggests a maintained ability to move around without assistive devices, handle routine tasks, and remain engaged in modest physical activity, limited mainly by the persistent knee discomfort. No sign points to a malignant process now or in the past, as prior screenings and regular check-ups have not detected suspicious findings. At present, the patient appears stable overall, though some lingering fatigue is noted, potentially linked to the recent neurological insult. Examination confirms that the joints demonstrate limited range of motion but no overt warmth or marked tenderness to palpation, aside from the expected discomfort in the affected knee. The plan to proceed with a small-incision, camera-assisted intervention is driven by the patient’s ongoing symptoms and the clinical consensus that this less extensive approach could improve joint function with a more rapid recovery compared to open procedures. The patient expresses awareness that the recent neurologic event warrants caution, but appears motivated to regain independence and address the knee issue before further functional decline. No features suggest new-onset infection, ongoing systemic instability, or other complications that would preclude operative management. Laboratory workup shows no unexpected deviations in blood counts or chemistries, and electrodiagnostic tests performed in relation to the neurologic episode indicate stabilization of the original deficit. Despite some concerns regarding operative risk, the patient remains optimistic and agrees to adhere strictly to perioperative instructions, including recommended precautions to support circulation and ensure the best possible outcome.
